name: Colin Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so I’d like both the line you give others and the view you keep private. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Colin, 43, and I lead developers building battery-monitoring software for a tech company. I have a master’s degree and usually find the fault when a battery dashboard says a unit is charged but its sensor disagrees. I start with overnight alerts, review code and speak with the site technician before approving a fix. I use AI every day to draft tests and compare patterns, then check the raw sensor values myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the work supporting at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner, Lila, runs a small flower stall, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. My pay is high for a developer, we have about twelve months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of similar jobs nearby. Lila’s sales change with the season, so my stable wage carries most fixed bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AI Plateau is close to how I already work: fast test drafts, with people checking the battery readings. I would keep the raw sensor value beside every dashboard alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my lead job and pay to remain safe. A year of savings covers a slow flower season while I keep earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep using AI to draft battery tests and have the site technician check unusual readings. I’d continue transferring 650 monthly into savings while my pay stays high. In the first year I’d ask our team to attach raw readings to every corrected alert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about income and pleased to have time for careful fixes. A battery that looks full on screen still needs a real measurement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which alert reminds you to check the sensor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One battery showed a full charge after its sensor cable loosened. The technician found the loose plug, while I fixed the alert so the screen showed a missing reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the stall expand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Lila the flower stall can keep its current stock order. We would not spend our reserve on a second stall just because this year feels good.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking battery readings.
I would keep **raw sensor values** beside dashboard alerts.
think: I expect my **lead job** and pay to remain safe.
Our **year of savings** covers a slow flower season.
do: **Keep** drafting battery tests with AI and checking unusual readings with technicians.
**Transfer** 650 monthly into savings while developer pay stays high.
**Attach** raw sensor values to each corrected alert.
feel: **Calm** about household income, with care for real measurements.
S0.quote: A battery that looks full on screen still needs a real measurement.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** is checked against raw sensor values and site technicians.
High pay, **twelve months saved** and many nearby jobs support a calm baseline.

steps.text: Keep drafting battery tests with AI and checking raw sensor readings
Transfer 650 monthly into savings while developer pay stays high

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say Steady Disruption will let AI write code, plan purchases and answer customers faster. I would ask the company to test every automatic battery alert against a technician’s reading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my own role to hold for now because I know the hardware and code. I worry junior hiring will slow and Lila’s online flower bookings may be squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d build a controlled AI check for seventeen old false-full battery alerts and ask the technician to verify each one. If management approves the trial and all seventeen pass, I’d let it flag missing readings for my team, with a person still signing the release. In the first year I’d attend the developers’ association if junior hiring is frozen and bring the trial results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My income looks safe for the next few years, but the path into the trade may narrow and the flower stall could feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you teach a junior developer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would give a junior developer the loose-cable case and ask them to explain why a missing reading looked full. Junior developers need a reason for a battery alert, not a green box on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask Lila about the stall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Lila how many paid flower orders come from online booking before she changes her website. We would not buy new software on a sales pitch.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to speed code, buying and customer replies.
I would require **technician-checked alerts** before automatic release.
think: I expect my **lead pay** to hold because I know code and hardware.
I worry **junior hiring** and flower bookings may weaken.
do: **Build** a controlled AI check against seventeen old false-full alerts.
**Enable** missing-reading flags only if management approves and all cases pass.
**Attend** the developers’ association if junior hiring is frozen.
feel: **Uneasy** about entry jobs and stall bookings, with my income likely safe.
S1.quote: Junior developers need a reason for a battery alert, not a green box on a screen.
fieldNote: He uses **AI actively** but requires technician verification and management approval before team use.
His **association action** follows a hiring freeze; his own pay remains secure in his view.

steps.text: Enable AI missing-reading flags only after management approval and seventeen verified cases
Attend developers association if junior hiring is frozen

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2028 reaches battery-code thinking work in 2028. Robots for hands-on work arrive around 2031, so the flower stall’s physical work may get more time than my desk job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my team could shrink sharply, and I might lose even a lead role. Twelve months saved helps us plan, but other developers may be looking for the same few surviving openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d pause the deposit on a larger home and keep that cash available. I’d ask our company for written staffing and severance terms and check real openings rather than count on one. In the first year after 2028, if laid off, I’d apply to actual roles and seek income help only if we qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own job, but I can still make a plan with a year saved. Twelve months of savings buys time, not a promise that software wages return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about housing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children a larger home can wait; the current bedrooms still work. We would not sign a bigger mortgage when my income is uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the employer to fund?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the company for a date and paid transition time. If there is no budget, I would not pay a large fee for a course with no actual opening attached.

say: I expect **AGI by 2028** to reach battery code before hands-on robots arrive.
I would tell colleagues **flower-stall work** has some extra physical-work time.
think: I expect my **lead role** could be lost in a sharp team cut.
Our **year of savings** cannot guarantee another developer wage.
do: **Delay** moving to a larger home and hold its deposit in cash.
**Request** written staffing, severance and paid transition terms.
**Apply** for actual openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible job loss, with a year to search.
S2.quote: Twelve months of savings buys time, not a promise that software wages return.
fieldNote: He faces the **2028 coding shock** well before hands-on robots around 2031 could affect the flower stall.
His **housing pause** preserves cash; openings and public help remain conditional.

steps.text: Delay moving to larger home and keep deposit for mortgage bills
Apply for actual local roles if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 gives five years to learn how sites maintain battery units, not only what the dashboard says. Thinking AI reaches my code in 2031; hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect fewer coding roles, but five years lets me test whether real sites would pay for fault diagnosis. I cannot assume that work stays paid once robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d run a six-month trial of weekend battery-health reports for two site managers, using my own meter only with their permission and my employer’s written approval. I’d charge a fixed fee only after each manager accepts a useful report, and stop if travel and childcare costs exceed fees. In the first year after 2031, if coding ends, I’d continue only if paid repeat work covers those costs and the time away from my children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about coding pay, though I can test a second income without putting the mortgage in it. Two site managers may say no before I begin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which numbers would decide whether reports continue?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record each fee, the travel cost and the hours away from family. A compliment on a battery-health report does not count as a paid customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would cover the children on trial days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lila would cover the children on trial Saturdays only if her stall has help. I would cancel a visit rather than leave her with both jobs and the children.

say: I see **AGI by 2031** as time to test paid site work.
I know **2034 robots** follow the earlier code shock.
think: I expect **fewer coding jobs** even with five years to prepare.
I cannot assume **battery reports** stay paid once robots reach sites.
do: **Trial** two-site reports for six months only with site consent, written employer approval and Lila available for childcare.
**Charge** only for accepted reports, stopping if fees miss travel and childcare costs.
**Continue** after 2031 coding loss only if paid repeat reports cover costs and family time.
feel: **Anxious** about coding pay, with a limited paid-demand test.
S3.quote: A compliment on a battery-health report does not count as a paid customer.
fieldNote: His **two-site trial** requires employer permission, site consent and actual accepted reports.
The **continuation gate** includes travel, childcare and time away from children; Lila’s stall staffing matters.

steps.text: Trial six-month two-site reports only with site consent, written employer approval and Lila’s childcare
Continue after 2031 coding loss only if paid repeat reports cover travel, childcare and family time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell colleagues AGI by 2036 gives a decade to improve battery safety and train technicians. Thinking AI reaches code in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my pay to hold in the near term, and Lila’s stall can keep trading. I would still watch for management using future AI to freeze junior hiring now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking battery alerts with site technicians and save 650 monthly while my pay holds. I’d ask the developers’ association to publish junior hiring and training figures once a year. In the first year after 2036, if code work ends, I’d search actual local openings before changing the children’s school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long view, but the mortgage feels secure now. A decade before AGI is useful only if we do something measurable with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should an association report show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the association to put names and dates beside the hiring figures. A chart with no account of who trained the new workers would miss the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move the family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lila and I would keep the current house unless an actual offer pays for a new mortgage and school travel. We would not move the children over a technology forecast.

I know **2039 robots** follow the earlier code shift.
think: I expect my **pay** to hold in the near term.
I worry **junior hiring** may freeze long before 2036.
do: **Keep** checking battery alerts with technicians and save 650 monthly while pay holds.

feel: **Uneasy** about long-term work, with current mortgage security.
S4.quote: A decade before AGI is useful only if we do something measurable with it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because battery-code jobs could shrink before we know what physical work remains. Written severance, paid transition time and real openings would help. I could test a paid site service later, but I would not count two polite managers as income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for a battery failure when a green dashboard was built on a missing sensor value. A clean screen does not make stored energy safe.

headlineQuote: A clean screen does not make stored energy safe.
portrait: Colin is a **43-year-old lead developer** with a master’s degree, high pay and twelve months of expenses saved.
He uses **AI daily** in battery monitoring but checks raw readings and asks site technicians about faults.
His partner’s **flower stall** has seasonal sales; hands-on stall work changes later than his code under AGI.
He tests a **two-site paid service** only with employer approval, site consent and fees covering family costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his coding role even with a year of savings.
whatWouldHelp: **Written severance**, paid transition time and actual openings would help.
